audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed initial' (initial stress) is confirmed by every source opened: Blake 1999 pp. 21-22, 25-26 (deciding quote verified verbatim in the PDF we hold/scanned), Blake 2000 PhD sec. 3.3.1 pp. 171-177 (held), Huijsmans 2022 p. 30 fn. 22 (held), Watanabe 2026 p. 100 (held), and the two 2023 ICSNL papers downloaded now (Menon, instrumental; McCarthy & Schnoor), all relaying Watanabe 2003: 21-29. No source suggests a different primary-stress position, so no reclassification. sources.citation: McCarthy, Mary & Tyler T. Schnoor. 2023. Yes/No Question Intonation in ʔayʔaǰuθəm. Papers for ICSNL 58, UBCWPL, pp. 333-339.
sources.quote: 'Primary word-level stress falls on the initial syllable in ʔayʔaǰuθəm. The assignment of secondary stress follows — with the exception of words containing certain suffixes — a left-aligned trochaic pattern in words that contain three or more syllables (Davis 1970; Watanabe 2003). Pitch is an important cue for stress (Watanabe 2003).'
sources.note: Recent summary of Watanabe 2003's stress description (initial primary, left-aligned trochaic secondary with suffix exceptions). downloaded now; confirms.

sources.citation: Menon, Aarya. 2023. A Phonetic Analysis of Stress Correlates and Stative Ambiguity in ʔayʔaǰuθəm. Papers for ICSNL 58, UBCWPL, pp. 340-347.
sources.quote: 'Primary stress in ʔayʔaǰuθəm occurs on the initial syllable, with the secondary stresses following a trochaic pattern (Blake 2000); secondary stress is assigned rightwards in alternating syllables ... some suffixes, such as the indirective (/-ʔəm/) appear to break this pattern by promoting themselves to take secondary stress (Watanabe 2003).' Instrumental result: duration (full vowels) / pitch (schwa) are the correlates of the initial primary stress; stative marked by raised pitch on the stressed vowel.
sources.note: Only instrumental study of word stress in the language; confirms initial primary stress and gives acoustic correlates. downloaded now.
